01-atomic-structure.q: The atomic number of an element is the number of…
options: protons and neutrons in the nucleus
01-atomic-structure.explain: Atomic number = protons only. Protons + neutrons is the mass number. The 2022 scheme explicitly ignored answers that added electrons.

01-atomic-structure.q: An atom has 14 protons, 14 electrons and 15 neutrons. Its mass number is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 14 + 15 = 29. Electrons weigh almost nothing and never count — 28 (protons + electrons) was a designed distractor on the 2022 paper.

01-atomic-structure.q: The particle in the atom with a relative mass of about 1/1836 is the…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Electrons are effectively massless; protons and neutrons each have relative mass 1 and make up all of the mass number.

01-atomic-structure.q: An atom of ¹¹₅B contains…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Bottom number = atomic number = 5 protons (and 5 electrons in a neutral atom); neutrons = 11 − 5 = 6. This was 2021 Q1.

01-atomic-structure.q: Isotopes of an element have the same number of…
options: neutrons and the same mass number
01-atomic-structure.explain: Same element = same protons; isotopes differ only in neutrons (so different mass numbers). Same electrons too — which is why their chemistry is identical.

01-atomic-structure.q: The electronic configuration of phosphorus (atomic number 15) is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Fill 2, then 8, then the rest: 15 electrons → 2.8.5. Asked as a one-marker in 2025.

01-atomic-structure.q: An element has the configuration 2.8.3. It is found in…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Group = outer electrons (3); period = occupied shells (3). The 2023 commentary said many students had "no concept" of period number — it counts the rows.

01-atomic-structure.q: The charge on the ion formed by an atom with configuration 2.8.1 is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: One outer electron is lost → +1 (this is sodium → Na⁺, 2.8). Answering just "positive" in 2023 scored nothing — the size of the charge is required.

01-atomic-structure.q: An element in Group 6 forms an ion with charge…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Group 6 atoms gain two electrons to complete the outer shell → 2− (like O²⁻). Groups 5/6/7 gain 3/2/1; Groups 1/2/3 lose 1/2/3.

01-atomic-structure.q: Copper is 69.5% ⁶³Cu and 30.5% ⁶⁵Cu. Its relative atomic mass is closest to…
01-atomic-structure.explain: (63 × 69.5 + 65 × 30.5) ÷ 100 = 63.61 → 63.6. A weighted mean always sits between the isotope masses, nearer the more abundant one — 64.0 is the unweighted average trap.

01-atomic-structure.q: Why do two isotopes of chlorine react identically?
options: They have the same number of neutrons
They have the same electronic configuration
They have the same mass number
01-atomic-structure.explain: Chemistry is decided by electrons. Isotopes have identical proton and electron counts and arrangements — only the neutrons (and mass) differ.

01-atomic-structure.q: The number of electrons available for bonding in a Group 8 (noble gas) element is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: A full outer shell means no tendency to lose, gain or share — zero bonding electrons, which is why noble gases are unreactive. This was 2024 Q1c.

01-atomic-structure.q: The part of the atom that contains almost all of its mass is the…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Protons and neutrons — all the mass — sit in the nucleus. Electrons orbit in shells and contribute essentially nothing to the mass.

01-atomic-structure.q: The electronic configuration of the chloride ion, Cl⁻ (chlorine has 17 electrons as an atom), is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: The ion has gained one electron: 18 → 2.8.8. Count the ion's actual electrons, not the atom's.

01-atomic-structure.q: Elements in the modern periodic table are arranged in order of…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Order of atomic number (protons). Ar mostly increases too but has exceptions — the definition the spec wants is atomic number.

01-atomic-structure.q: The mass number of an atom is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Mass number counts the heavy particles in the nucleus: protons + neutrons.

01-atomic-structure.q: An atom is electrically neutral because…
options: the numbers of protons and electrons are equal
01-atomic-structure.explain: Equal protons (+) and electrons (−) cancel. Neutrons are neutral and cancel nothing.

01-atomic-structure.q: ⁶³Cu and ⁶⁵Cu differ in their number of…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Isotopes: same protons and electrons, different neutrons — 34 versus 36 here.

01-atomic-structure.q: The electronic configuration of calcium (atomic number 20) is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Fill 2, 8, 8, then the remainder: 2.8.8.2. The third shell takes 8 for the first twenty elements.

01-atomic-structure.q: An element in Period 2 has…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Period = number of occupied shells. Two outer electrons would put it in Group 2 — the classic mix-up.

01-atomic-structure.q: The ion formed by aluminium (2.8.3) is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Group 3 metals lose all three outer electrons → 3+, leaving configuration 2.8.

01-atomic-structure.q: Which particle has a relative charge of 0?
01-atomic-structure.explain: Neutron = neutral, mass 1. Proton +1, electron −1.

01-atomic-structure.q: The number of neutrons in ⁵⁶₂₆Fe is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 56 − 26 = 30.

01-atomic-structure.q: Two atoms are the same element if they have the same number of…
01-atomic-structure.explain: The proton count defines the element — it fixes the atomic number and the electron count.

01-atomic-structure.q: A molecule is…
options: the smallest particle of an element
two or more atoms covalently bonded together
01-atomic-structure.explain: Atoms covalently bonded — O₂, H₂O, CH₄. A charged atom is an ion.

01-atomic-structure.q: Boron is 20% ¹⁰B and 80% ¹¹B. Its Ar is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: (10 × 20 + 11 × 80) ÷ 100 = 10.8 — nearer 11, the abundant isotope. 10.5 is the unweighted-average trap.

01-atomic-structure.q: An atom with configuration 2.8.7 will form an ion by…
01-atomic-structure.explain: One short of a full shell — gaining one is far easier than losing seven. Charge: 1− (this is chlorine).

01-atomic-structure.q: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar chemistry because they have…
options: the same number of outer electrons
01-atomic-structure.explain: Chemistry is set by outer electrons, and group number = outer electron count.

01-atomic-structure.q: The atomic number of an element with configuration 2.8.6 is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: 2 + 8 + 6 = 16 electrons = 16 protons (sulfur).

01-atomic-structure.q: Which statement about the nucleus is correct?
options: It contains nearly all the atom's mass
01-atomic-structure.explain: Protons + neutrons live there, so nearly all the mass does too; its charge is positive; chemistry happens in the electron shells.

01-atomic-structure.q: The ion O²⁻ has how many electrons? [oxygen's atomic number = 8]
01-atomic-structure.explain: The atom's 8 plus 2 gained = 10 (configuration 2.8).

01-atomic-structure.q: Magnesium is in Group 2, Period 3. Its electronic configuration is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Period 3 = three shells; Group 2 = two outer electrons: 2.8.2.

01-atomic-structure.q: Why is the relative atomic mass of an element sometimes not a whole number?
options: It is a weighted average over the natural isotopes
01-atomic-structure.explain: Every atom has whole-number mass; the natural MIX averages to something in between — chlorine's 35.5 from ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl.

01-atomic-structure.q: An atom of potassium (2.8.8.1) sits in…
01-atomic-structure.explain: One outer electron → Group 1; four occupied shells → Period 4.

01-atomic-structure.q: Which pair are isotopes?
01-atomic-structure.explain: Same element (6 protons), different mass numbers. Na/Mg are different elements; an atom and its own ion are not isotopes; two identical atoms are just the same atom.

01-atomic-structure.q: The maximum number of electrons in the first shell is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: First shell holds 2; the second and third hold 8 each (for the first 20 elements).

01-atomic-structure.q: A neutral atom loses two electrons. The particle formed is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Losing negatives leaves a 2+ ion. Gaining two would give 2−.

01-atomic-structure.q: The Group 7 elements are called…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Group 7 = halogens (F, Cl, Br, I); Group 1 = alkali metals; Group 8/0 = noble gases.

01-atomic-structure.q: Ar for an element is measured relative to…
01-atomic-structure.explain: The modern scale sets ¹²C = 12 exactly; everything else is relative to it.

01-atomic-structure.q: Which is the correct order of size, smallest first?
01-atomic-structure.explain: The nucleus is a tiny core of the atom; molecules are two or more atoms.

01-atomic-structure.q: 34.60% of copper pyrites is copper (Ar 63.5). In an empirical-formula calculation, the first step for copper is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Mass ÷ Ar converts to moles of atoms. Upside-down or atomic-number divisions score 0/3 on the school's schemes.

01-atomic-structure.q: An element X forms X²⁻ ions with configuration 2.8.8. X's atomic number is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: The ion has 18 electrons, two more than the atom: 16 protons (sulfur).

01-atomic-structure.q: How many electrons are in the outer shell of a Group 5 element?
01-atomic-structure.explain: Group number = outer electrons; Group 5 atoms gain three to reach a full shell (→ 3− ions like N³⁻ and P³⁻).

01-atomic-structure.q: The noble gases are unreactive because…
01-atomic-structure.explain: A full outer shell means no drive to lose, gain or share electrons — and they go around as single atoms, not diatomic molecules.

01-atomic-structure.q: Which statement correctly compares ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl?
options: ³⁷Cl is heavier but chemically identical
01-atomic-structure.explain: Two extra NEUTRONS add mass but leave the electron arrangement — and therefore the chemistry — unchanged.

01-atomic-structure.q: Which particle determines which element an atom is?
01-atomic-structure.explain: The proton count is the atomic number, and that defines the element. Change the neutrons and you get an isotope; change the electrons and you get an ion — still the same element.

01-atomic-structure.q: An ion has 12 protons and 10 electrons. Its charge is…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Two more positives than negatives → 2+. This is Mg²⁺ (magnesium, atomic number 12).

01-atomic-structure.q: The electrons in the outer shell of an atom are important because they…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Bonding and reactions are all outer-shell electrons — which is why the group number (= outer electrons) predicts chemistry so well.

01-atomic-structure.q: Which element has the electronic configuration 2.8.8?
01-atomic-structure.explain: 18 electrons = argon, a Group 8 noble gas with a full outer shell. Neon is 2.8; chlorine 2.8.7; potassium 2.8.8.1.

01-atomic-structure.q: Going ACROSS a period from left to right, the number of occupied shells…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Across a period the shell count is fixed and outer electrons build up; DOWN a group a new shell is added each time.

01-atomic-structure.q: An atom of ³⁹₁₉K contains…
01-atomic-structure.explain: Bottom = protons (19), so 19 electrons in a neutral atom; neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20.

01-atomic-structure.q: Which statement about electrons is TRUE?
options: They are found in the nucleus
They have a relative mass of 1
They occupy shells around the nucleus
01-atomic-structure.explain: Shells (energy levels) around the nucleus; relative mass ≈ 1/1836; charge −1. Only protons and neutrons live in the nucleus.

01-atomic-structure.q: The relative atomic mass of magnesium is 24.3, not a whole number, because…
options: it is a weighted average of magnesium's isotopes
01-atomic-structure.explain: Natural magnesium is a mixture of ²⁴Mg, ²⁵Mg and ²⁶Mg; the average sits just above 24 because the lightest isotope dominates.

01-atomic-structure.q: Which pair of ions both have the electronic configuration 2.8?
01-atomic-structure.explain: Na (2.8.1) loses one → 2.8; F (2.7) gains one → 2.8. Both reach the neon configuration — this is what 'full outer shell' means in practice.

01-atomic-structure.q: Which is NOT a reason the periodic table is arranged as it is?
options: Elements are in order of atomic number
Elements in a group have the same number of outer electrons
Elements in a period have the same number of shells
01-atomic-structure.explain: Density plays no part. Order = atomic number; columns share outer-electron count; rows share shell count.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: An ionic bond is best described as…
options: the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: The transfer creates the ions; the BOND is the attraction between them. Sharing is covalent; weak intermolecular forces are not bonds at all.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: When magnesium (2.8.2) bonds with oxygen (2.6), what happens?
options: Each Mg shares two electrons with O
Each Mg loses two electrons and each O gains two
Each Mg gains two electrons and each O loses two
Electrons are transferred from oxygen to magnesium
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Metal loses, non-metal gains — and the number matters: two each. The 2023 scheme refused marks for "electrons moved" without saying how many.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: A covalent bond holds two atoms together because…
options: the shared pair of electrons is attracted to the nucleus
the shared pair of electrons is attracted to the nuclei of both atoms
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Nuclei — plural. Both 2021 and 2022 refused the mark when only one nucleus was mentioned.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Hydrogen has very strong H–H bonds but boils at −253 °C. Why?
options: There are only weak forces between the molecules
Hydrogen molecules are very small ions
The bonds are weakened by heating
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Boiling separates molecules; it never breaks covalent bonds. The 2021 scheme scored any bond-breaking answer 0/2 — the weak intermolecular forces are the whole story.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Sodium chloride conducts electricity when molten because…
options: its electrons become free to move
its ions become free to move
it becomes a metal when heated
molten salts always contain free atoms
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Ionic conduction is always ions moving. Electron answers score zero — electrons carry charge in metals and graphite, not in molten salts.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Which substance has a giant covalent structure?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Diamond is a continuous covalent network. CO₂ and C₆₀ are simple molecular (C₆₀ is the classic trap — 60 atoms, but still discrete molecules); NaCl is giant ionic.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Magnesium oxide has a high melting point because…
options: strong covalent bonds must be broken
strong intermolecular forces must be overcome
there is a strong attraction between oppositely charged ions
the molecules are held in a rigid lattice
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Giant ionic lattice: strong electrostatic attraction between opposite ions needs lots of energy. In 2025 any mention of covalent bonds, molecules or IMF scored 0/3.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Graphite conducts electricity because…
options: its ions are free to move
its layers can slide over each other
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Each carbon bonds to only three others, freeing one electron per atom — delocalised between the layers. Sliding layers explain softness, not conduction.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: C₆₀ fullerene melts far below graphite because…
options: melting it only overcomes intermolecular forces between molecules
it contains fewer carbon atoms per bond
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: C₆₀ is simple molecular — the balls separate without breaking a single bond. Graphite is giant covalent, so melting it breaks covalent bonds, which costs far more energy.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: The two types of particle in a metallic structure are…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: A lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. "Protons" was explicitly rejected in 2025 — the labels are ions and electrons.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Metals are malleable because…
options: intermolecular forces between atoms are weak
the delocalised electrons repel each other
layers of ions can slide over one another
the metallic bonds break when hammered
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Layers slide and the electron sea keeps binding them in the new position. Intermolecular-force answers were rejected — there are no molecules in a metal.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: A substance melts at −101 °C and never conducts electricity. Its structure is…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Low melting point + no conduction in any state = simple molecular. Ionic conducts when molten; metals conduct always; giant covalent has a huge melting point.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Calcium phosphide has the formula Ca₃P₂ because…
options: calcium shares three electrons with phosphorus
three Ca²⁺ ions balance two P³⁻ ions
two Ca³⁺ ions balance three P²⁻ ions
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Ca²⁺ (Group 2) and P³⁻ (Group 5): 3 × (2+) = 6+ balances 2 × (3−) = 6−. Any sharing-based answer scored zero in 2025 — metal + non-metal is ionic.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Which statement about ionic compounds is correct?
options: They conduct when molten or dissolved in water
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: The ions must be free to move: molten or in solution. In the solid they are locked in the lattice.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: In a dot-and-cross diagram of N₂, the number of shared electrons is…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Nitrogen needs three more electrons each → a triple bond: three shared pairs = six electrons, plus one lone pair on each atom. 2022's M1 was exactly "6 bonding electrons".

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Ionic bonding occurs between…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Metal loses electrons, non-metal gains: ions form and attract. Non-metal + non-metal share instead (covalent).

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Covalent bonding occurs between…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Two non-metals both need electrons, so they share pairs.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: In a dot-and-cross diagram of HCl, chlorine keeps how many lone pairs?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: One of chlorine's seven outer electrons is in the shared pair; the other six form three lone pairs.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: The formula of the compound formed from Na⁺ and O²⁻ is…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Two 1+ ions balance one 2− ion: Na₂O.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: When sodium reacts with chlorine, each sodium atom…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Metal atoms lose their outer electrons; sodium's single outer electron transfers to chlorine. Protons never move in chemistry.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity because…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: The ions are there but locked in the lattice. Free them (melt or dissolve) and it conducts.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Diamond is extremely hard because…
options: each carbon is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid network
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: A giant covalent network with every atom pinned by four strong bonds. Layers belong to graphite; delocalised electrons too.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Graphite is soft and slippery because…
options: its layers can slide over each other
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Strong bonds within each layer, weak attraction between layers — they slide, which is why it works as a lubricant and pencil lead.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Which substance does NOT conduct electricity in any state?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Covalent molecules: no ions, no delocalised electrons, nothing to carry charge. The other three all conduct.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: The melting points of the halogens increase down the group because…
options: the intermolecular forces between larger molecules are stronger
they gain more electrons in bonds
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Bigger molecules → stronger IMF → more energy to separate them. The bonds inside each molecule are irrelevant to melting.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Ice melts at 0 °C but salt melts at 801 °C. The best explanation is…
options: melting ice overcomes weak intermolecular forces; melting salt overcomes strong ionic attractions
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Simple molecular vs giant ionic — different structures, different particles being separated, hugely different energies.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: The particles at the lattice points of a metal are…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: The outer electrons have left to join the delocalised sea, leaving positive ions in the lattice.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Metals conduct electricity because…
options: their delocalised electrons can move through the structure
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: The electron sea drifts when a voltage is applied. Sliding layers explain malleability, not conduction.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: An unknown solid melts at 3550 °C and never conducts. It is most likely…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Huge melting point rules out molecular; no conduction ever rules out metal and (molten) ionic. Diamond fits exactly.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: An unknown solid conducts when molten but not when solid. It is…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: The signature of an ionic compound: ions locked when solid, free when molten.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: How many electrons does each nitrogen atom contribute to the triple bond in N₂?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Three shared pairs = six electrons total, three from each atom.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: The formula of the ionic compound formed from Al³⁺ and O²⁻ is…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Charges must cancel: 2 × (3+) = 3 × (2−) = 6 each way → Al₂O₃.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Which of these is a property of MOST metals?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Sliding layers make them malleable; delocalised electrons make them conduct.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: In magnesium oxide, the ions present are…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Group 2 loses two, Group 6 gains two — a 1:1 compound of doubly charged ions (which is why MgO's melting point is so high).

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Why does C₆₀ fullerene dissolve in some solvents while graphite dissolves in none?
options: C₆₀ consists of separate molecules that can be surrounded by solvent
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Discrete molecules can be pried apart by solvent (only IMF to overcome); a giant covalent network cannot be dissolved without breaking bonds.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: When magnesium burns in oxygen, the product's bonding is…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Metal + non-metal → electron transfer → ionic MgO.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: The attraction holding a metallic lattice together is between…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: That ion–electron attraction IS metallic bonding.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Which substance is a gas at room temperature?
options: A substance with mp −101 °C and bp −35 °C
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Room temperature (~20 °C) is above its boiling point, so it is a gas — the simple molecular pattern from 2021's table.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: A dot-and-cross diagram of water (H₂O) shows oxygen with…
options: two bonding pairs and two lone pairs
one bonding pair and three lone pairs
two bonding pairs and no lone pairs
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Two O–H shared pairs; oxygen's remaining four electrons sit as two lone pairs.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Why must an ionic-melting-point answer avoid the word "molecule"?
options: A giant ionic lattice contains no molecules — the word signals the wrong model and scores 0
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: 2025's scheme: covalent/molecule/IMF language in the ionic answer = 0/3. Giant structures are continuous — no molecules anywhere.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Which shows the ions in calcium chloride?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Ca²⁺ needs two 1− chloride ions: CaCl₂. Metals form positive ions, non-metals negative.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Graphite is used as an electrode material because it…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Delocalised electrons carry the current, and it survives the chemistry — the same reason it appears in the electrolysis module.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: The bonding within one layer of graphite is…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Each carbon covalently bonds to three neighbours within the layer; only the BETWEEN-layer attraction is weak.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Substance X conducts electricity as a solid and can be hammered flat. X is…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Solid-state conduction + malleability is the metallic fingerprint (graphite conducts but is brittle and flaky).

02-bonding-and-structures.q: How many atoms are in one molecule of C₆₀ fullerene?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Sixty carbons per ball — large, but still a fixed, countable molecule, which is exactly why it behaves as simple molecular.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Which type of bonding involves a transfer of electrons?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Ionic: metal transfers to non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions that attract. Covalent shares; metallic pools electrons.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: How many covalent bonds does a carbon atom normally form?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Four outer electrons, four bonds — the rule that makes every organic displayed formula checkable: if a carbon has fewer than four bonds, the drawing is wrong.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: In a dot-and-cross diagram of methane, CH₄, the carbon has…
options: four bonding pairs and no lone pairs
two bonding pairs and two lone pairs
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: All four outer electrons are used in C–H bonds, so no lone pairs remain on carbon.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Why does sodium chloride have a much higher melting point than chlorine gas?
options: It has a giant ionic lattice with strong attractions between ions, not weak forces between molecules
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Structure decides everything: giant ionic vs simple molecular. Never explain an ionic melting point with covalent or intermolecular language — 2025 scored that 0.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Substance X conducts electricity when dissolved in water but not as a solid. X is…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Dissolving frees the ions to move. Metals conduct as solids; simple molecular substances never conduct; graphite conducts as a solid.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: In C₆₀ fullerene, what is overcome when it melts?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: The balls separate; every covalent bond inside them survives. That is exactly why it melts far below giant covalent graphite.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Which substance contains delocalised electrons?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Graphite (and all metals). Each carbon bonds to only three others, leaving one electron per atom free — hence graphite conducts, unlike diamond.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Why can a metal be drawn into a wire?
options: Layers of positive ions slide over one another while the bonding survives
Its molecules are long and thin
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: Ductility and malleability are both the sliding-layers story. Ionic crystals shatter instead because sliding brings like charges together.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Which pairing of substance and structure is WRONG?
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: CO₂ is SIMPLE MOLECULAR — small discrete molecules, which is why it is a gas at room temperature. Silicon dioxide is the giant covalent oxide.

02-bonding-and-structures.q: Two atoms share two pairs of electrons. This is a…
02-bonding-and-structures.explain: One shared pair = single, two = double (as in O₂ and CO₂), three = triple (as in N₂, six shared electrons).

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The formula of magnesium nitride is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Mg²⁺ and N³⁻: three magnesiums (6+) balance two nitrides (6−). This was one of 2024's ion-table answers.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The formula of ammonium carbonate is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: NH₄⁺ and CO₃²⁻ — two ammoniums per carbonate, with brackets because a molecular ion is being multiplied.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which of these is written correctly?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Element symbols keep their own capitalisation: H + Br = HBr. The 2024 scheme rejected HBR and hbr outright — case is chemistry.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which element does NOT exist as diatomic molecules?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: The diatomic seven are H₂ N₂ O₂ F₂ Cl₂ Br₂ I₂. Noble gases like neon go around as single atoms.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: To balance Mg + O₂ → MgO you should…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Balancing changes only the big numbers in front. Editing a subscript (MgO₂) invents a different substance — formulae are fixed by the ion charges.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: In Ca₃(PO₄)₂ the total number of oxygen atoms is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: The bracket multiplies everything inside: 2 × 4 = 8 oxygens. This count is why the phosphide equation needs 8C and 8CO.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The state symbol for zinc nitrate formed in solution from zinc + dilute nitric acid is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: A soluble salt (all nitrates are soluble) stays dissolved where it formed — (aq). 2024's commentary: many wrongly wrote (s) or (l).

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The state symbol for the water produced in a neutralisation is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Pure water is the liquid itself: (l). (aq) means dissolved IN water — water cannot be dissolved in itself.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Balanced correctly, ethane burning completely in air is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: 4 C, 12 H, 14 O each side. Option A shorts the oxygen (needs 3.5, not 3) — doubling everything fixes it.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: A compound ending in -ate always contains…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: -ate = the element plus oxygen (sulfate SO₄²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻). -ide means just the element itself.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The charge on the iron ion in iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₃, is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: The Roman numeral states the charge: iron(III) = Fe³⁺ — balanced by three OH⁻. Iron is the classic two-charge metal: Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which equation for the thermite reaction is correct?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Formulae first (Fe₂O₃, Al₂O₃), then balance: two aluminiums, two irons. 2024's commentary: "many got close but did not include balancing numbers."

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The relative formula mass of Na₃N is… [Na = 23, N = 14]
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: 3 × 23 + 14 = 83. The commonest slip is forgetting to multiply the sodium by three.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which pair of ions produces a compound with the formula X₂Y?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Two 1+ ions balance one 2− ion: X₂Y (like Na₂O or (NH₄)₂SO₄). X²⁺ with Y⁻ gives XY₂ — the mirror-image trap.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: In a balanced equation, what must be the same on both sides?
options: The number of atoms of each element
The total of the big numbers
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Atoms are conserved — that is the whole meaning of balancing. Molecule counts can change freely (4 molecules → 3 is fine).

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The formula of calcium nitrate is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Ca²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻ ions, bracketed before multiplying: Ca(NO₃)₂.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The formula of iron(II) sulfate is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Iron(II) = Fe²⁺, which balances one SO₄²⁻ exactly. Fe₂(SO₄)₃ is iron(III) sulfate.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The charge on the sulfate ion is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: SO₄²⁻. The 2− is why sodium sulfate is Na₂SO₄ and magnesium sulfate is just MgSO₄.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which formula is wrong?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Hydroxide is a molecular ion, so it needs brackets when doubled: Mg(OH)₂. Without them the formula reads one O and two H.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The word equation for zinc + hydrochloric acid is…
options: zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + water
zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen
zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc hydroxide + chlorine
zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc + hydrogen chloride
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Water comes from acid + base, not acid + metal.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Balancing CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O correctly gives…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Four hydrogens need 2H₂O; total oxygen on the right is 4 atoms = 2O₂.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: In the equation 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe, the big 2 in "2Al" means…
options: two aluminium ATOMS react per formula unit of iron oxide
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Coefficients count particles; subscripts describe what a particle is. 2Al = two separate atoms of aluminium.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which substance's formula includes brackets?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: (NH₄)₂SO₄ — a molecular ion multiplied needs brackets. NaOH has only one OH, so none are needed.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The state symbol (aq) means…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Aqueous = in water solution. A pure liquid is (l) — the distinction the papers test with water itself.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: In CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g), the (s) tells you calcium carbonate is…
options: a precipitate formed in the reaction
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: It enters as solid marble — carbonates (except Na/K/NH₄) are insoluble.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: How many oxygen atoms are in 3Ca(NO₃)₂?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Each Ca(NO₃)₂ has 2 × 3 = 6 oxygens; three of them = 18. Coefficients multiply the whole formula.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The correct formula for hydrogen gas in an equation is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Elemental hydrogen is diatomic: H₂. Lone H atoms don't exist free; H⁺ is an ion in solution.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The products of any acid + metal carbonate reaction are…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: The carbonate fizzes CO₂, and water forms too — three products, always.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which is the correct formula of ammonia?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Ammonia the molecule is NH₃; ammonium the ion is NH₄⁺ — one letter of difference the papers exploit.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Balancing Ca₃P₂ + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + PH₃ correctly gives…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: 3 Ca and 2 P fix the right side; count H: 3×2 + 2×3 = 12 = 6H₂O. The 2025 two-marker.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: An -ide ending (as in sodium chloride) tells you the compound contains…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: -ide = just the elements named. -ate adds oxygen (chlorate, sulfate, nitrate).

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The formula of copper(II) nitrate is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Cu²⁺ + two NO₃⁻ → Cu(NO₃)₂. NO₂⁻ would be nitrite — wrong ion.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which equation is NOT balanced?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: The thermite needs 2Al and 2Fe. Recount every element — the aluminium and iron are both short.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The total number of atoms in one formula unit of (NH₄)₂SO₄ is…
Silver nitrate solution reacting with sodium chloride solution is written…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Two solutions in, insoluble silver chloride precipitates (s), soluble sodium nitrate stays (aq).

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which ion has a 3− charge?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Nitride N³⁻ (Group 5 gains three). Nitrate NO₃⁻ is 1−; sulfate 2−; chloride 1−.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: To balance an equation you may change…
options: the coefficients in front of formulae
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Only the big numbers. Everything else changes the chemistry itself.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The equation for magnesium burning is 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). Why is MgO given (s)?
options: It forms as a solid (white powder)
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: State symbols describe each substance as it actually is: MgO forms as white solid ash.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Fe³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ combine to give…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6: two Fe³⁺ (6+) balance three SO₄²⁻ (6−).

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The number of hydrogen atoms in 2NH₃ is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: 2 × 3 = 6. The coefficient multiplies every atom in the formula.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The formula of aluminium oxide is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Al³⁺ and O²⁻: two aluminiums (6+) balance three oxides (6−).

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The formula of sodium carbonate is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Na⁺ with CO₃²⁻ needs two sodiums. No brackets are needed — the carbonate appears only once.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: How many atoms in total are in Ca(OH)₂?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: 1 Ca + 2 O + 2 H = 5. The bracket multiplies BOTH atoms inside it — forgetting the hydrogens is the classic Mr slip.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which is the correctly balanced equation?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: 4 H and 2 O on each side. Option A has two oxygens on the left and one on the right.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The state symbol for a precipitate formed when two solutions are mixed is…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: It is an insoluble SOLID, even though it formed inside a liquid — (s). Everything still dissolved stays (aq).

03-formulae-and-equations.q: In the equation 3Ca(OH)₂, how many oxygen atoms are there?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Each formula unit has 2 oxygens; three of them = 6. Coefficient × bracket contents.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: The word equation for a metal carbonate reacting with an acid gives…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Three products, and the CO₂ is what you see fizzing. Metal + acid gives hydrogen instead; base + acid gives just salt + water.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which formula correctly represents iron(III) oxide?
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Fe³⁺ with O²⁻: two irons (6+) to three oxides (6−). FeO would be iron(II) oxide — the Roman numeral is the instruction.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Balancing Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃ requires…
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: 4 Fe and 6 O each side. When an odd number of oxygens appears in the product, doubling the product usually resolves it.

03-formulae-and-equations.q: Which change is NOT allowed when balancing an equation?
options: Putting a 2 in front of a formula
03-formulae-and-equations.explain: Editing a subscript invents a different substance (hydrogen peroxide, not water). Only the numbers in FRONT may change.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: An acid in aqueous solution is a source of…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Acids release H⁺ in solution (they are proton donors). Alkalis release OH⁻. This one-liner is a recurring one-mark question — 2021 asked it about SO₂ solution.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The colour of methyl orange in dilute hydrochloric acid is…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in alkali. Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in alkali. Litmus: red/blue.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: A base that is soluble in water is called…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Alkali = soluble base (NaOH, KOH). All alkalis are bases; most bases (metal oxides, most hydroxides) never dissolve.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The salt produced from zinc and dilute sulfuric acid is…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: The acid decides the salt's surname: sulfuric → sulfates, hydrochloric → chlorides, nitric → nitrates. Sulfide (-ide) would mean just zinc + sulfur.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which of these salts is insoluble in water?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are always soluble. Lead(II) is an exception in both the chloride and sulfate rules — PbBr₂ is the school's favourite insoluble salt.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Mixing which pair of solutions produces a precipitate?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Swap the partners and check the rules: calcium carbonate is insoluble → precipitate. In the other three, every product is soluble — nothing happens. This was 2024 Q2b.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: In the excess-solid method for a soluble salt, the excess is used so that…
options: all the acid is used up
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Left-over acid would contaminate the crystals and cannot be filtered out; left-over solid can. "To make more salt" misses the logic — 2024's one-marker was "so all the acid reacts".

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: When preparing hydrated crystals, the filtrate should be heated…
options: until crystals just start to form, then cooled
with a Bunsen at full roar until it spits
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Heat to the crystallisation point only, then cool and crystallise. Heating to dryness caps the answer at 1 mark — it destroys the water of crystallisation.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: In a precipitation reaction, the salt you want ends up…
options: as the residue on the filter paper
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: The insoluble product is the residue — wash THAT with distilled water and dry it. 2023's commentary: students washing the filtrate had it exactly backwards.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The correct final step for drying a precipitate is…
options: heat it strongly with a Bunsen burner
leave it in a warm oven or pat with filter paper
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Gentle drying only — the 2022 scheme explicitly rejected direct Bunsen heating of the product.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Copper(II) sulfate solution is mixed with sodium hydroxide solution. What would you SEE?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Copper(II) hydroxide is an insoluble blue solid. No gas is made, so fizzing is wrong — 2023 rejected it. Hydroxides are insoluble except sodium, potassium (and calcium slightly).

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which acid and alkali make potassium chloride?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Chloride needs hydrochloric acid; potassium needs the potassium alkali. Both reactants are soluble, so the titration method is used — no excess to filter.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The observation when magnesium ribbon is added to dilute acid is…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: An observation is what you SEE: bubbles and the metal disappearing. "Hydrogen is given off" is a deduction — the schemes ignore it as an observation.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which method should be used to prepare pure barium sulfate?
options: Excess barium + sulfuric acid, then filter
Titration of barium hydroxide with sulfuric acid
Mix two soluble solutions, filter, wash the residue, dry
Evaporate a solution of barium sulfate to dryness
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: BaSO₄ is insoluble — precipitation is the only correct method. There is no such thing as "a solution of barium sulfate" to evaporate, and describing a soluble-salt method scores at most 1.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: In terms of protons, an acid is…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Acid = proton (H⁺) donor; base = proton acceptor. Neutralisation is one proton handed from acid to base: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The pH of a strongly acidic solution is…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: 0–3 strong acid · 4–6 weak acid · 7 neutral · 8–10 weak alkali · 11–14 strong alkali — the spec's own bands.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Phenolphthalein in an alkaline solution is…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Colourless in acid, pink in alkali — the sharpest of the three named indicators.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Universal indicator is more useful than litmus because it…
options: shows the approximate pH, not just acid or alkali
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Its colour sweep maps to the pH scale; litmus only answers acid-or-alkali.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The ionic equation for every neutralisation is…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Acid's proton meets base's hydroxide, making water. Everything else is spectators.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which oxide would neutralise hydrochloric acid?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Metal oxides are bases. Non-metal oxides (CO₂, SO₂) are acidic — they'd make things worse.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The salt made from copper(II) oxide + sulfuric acid is…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Base + acid → salt + water; sulfuric acid makes sulfates. The classic blue solution.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which salt is soluble in water?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Ammonium salts are always soluble. AgCl, BaSO₄, CaCO₃ are the rules' three most-quoted insolubles.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which salt is INSOLUBLE in water?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Chlorides are soluble EXCEPT silver and lead(II). Nitrates: all soluble; Na/K salts: always.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: To make copper(II) sulfate crystals you add excess copper(II) oxide to warm sulfuric acid. The next step is…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Remove the excess solid first, then heat the filtrate to the crystallisation point, cool, and dry.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Hydrated crystals lose their water of crystallisation if you…
options: heat the solution to complete dryness
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Boiling everything off drives out the water bound in the crystal — the reason "heated to dryness" answers cap at 1 mark.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: In the titration method for potassium chloride, the indicator is used to…
options: find the exact volumes for neutralisation
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: It finds the end-point; the reaction is then repeated with those volumes WITHOUT the indicator so the salt is uncontaminated.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Mixing barium chloride solution with sodium sulfate solution produces…
options: a white precipitate of barium sulfate
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Swap partners: BaSO₄ (insoluble — precipitates, white) and NaCl (soluble). Sulfates' exceptions: Ba, Ca, Pb.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The precipitate is washed with distilled water to…
options: remove the soluble by-product clinging to it
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: The rinse carries away sodium nitrate (or similar) left in the wet solid; the insoluble product can't wash away.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Farmers add lime (calcium hydroxide) to soil to…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: A base neutralises acid soil — everyday neutralisation, a favourite context question.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which pair reacts WITHOUT producing a gas?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Alkali + acid → salt + water only. Metals give hydrogen; carbonates give CO₂.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The test for carbon dioxide is…
options: squeaky pop with a lit splint
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: CO₂ + limewater → milky/cloudy. The other three are H₂, O₂ and Cl₂ respectively.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: "Effervescence" means…
options: bubbling / fizzing as gas is produced
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: The word the schemes want for visible gas production — an observation, unlike naming the gas.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Ammonia solution is…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Ammonia is one of the spec's three named bases (metal oxides, metal hydroxides, ammonia) — it accepts protons.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The method for pure dry copper(II) hydroxide from copper sulfate + sodium hydroxide solutions is…
options: mix, filter, wash the residue, dry
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: It is a precipitation — the product is insoluble. Crystallisation methods belong to soluble salts only.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Why can't you make pure sodium chloride by adding excess sodium hydroxide to hydrochloric acid and filtering?
options: Excess NaOH is soluble and cannot be filtered out
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Both reactants are soluble — the leftover alkali stays dissolved and contaminates the salt. That is exactly why the titration method exists.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The reaction between an acid and a metal hydroxide produces…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Hydroxides are bases: neutralisation, water as the co-product. Hydrogen needs a metal; CO₂ needs a carbonate.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Nitric acid should NOT be used with which reactant type, according to the spec?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: The spec excludes nitric acid + metals (it misbehaves — no clean hydrogen). Use HCl or H₂SO₄ in metal examples.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: A student's salt crystals taste... — actually, what should a student NEVER do with a prepared salt?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Never taste lab chemicals. (And yes, safety one-markers do appear on school papers.)

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which observation shows neutralisation is complete when adding acid to alkali with universal indicator?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Green = pH 7 = neutral. Purple means still alkaline; keep adding acid.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: The proton-transfer description of neutralisation says the base…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Acid = proton donor; base = proton acceptor. The H⁺ moves from acid to base (OH⁻ → H₂O).

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which pH value indicates a strongly alkaline solution?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: 11–14 is strongly alkaline; 8–10 weakly alkaline; 7 neutral; 4–6 weakly acidic; 0–3 strongly acidic.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Adding an acid to an alkali until the solution is neutral means the resulting solution contains…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Neutralisation consumes both: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, leaving the salt dissolved in water.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which acid produces nitrate salts?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: The acid names the salt: nitric → nitrates, hydrochloric → chlorides, sulfuric → sulfates.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which substance would neutralise an acidic soil?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: A base — lime, calcium hydroxide. NaCl is a neutral salt and CO₂ dissolves to make things slightly more acidic.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: In a precipitation reaction, the two starting substances must both be…
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Mix two SOLUTIONS so the ions can meet; the insoluble combination drops out as the precipitate. The 2025 scheme rejected mixing solids.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which salt could be made by the excess-solid method with sulfuric acid?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Copper(II) oxide/carbonate is insoluble, so the excess filters off. Sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds are soluble — those need the titration route.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Why is the crystallising solution NOT boiled dry when making hydrated crystals?
options: The water of crystallisation would be driven off and impurities baked in
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: You lose the hydrated crystal structure and concentrate impurities onto the dish. Heat only to the crystallisation point, then cool.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: What is observed when a carbonate is added to dilute acid?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: CO₂ fizzes off (and turns limewater milky). 'Effervescence' is the observation word the schemes want.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: In the titration method, why is the experiment repeated without the indicator?
options: So the salt produced is not contaminated by the indicator
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: You need the volumes, not the dye. Repeat with the same measured volumes and no indicator, then crystallise a pure salt.

04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.q: Which combination would NOT produce a salt?
04-acids-alkalis-and-salts.explain: Salts come from an ACID plus something basic. Two bases together do nothing — there is no acid to donate the protons.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The amount, in moles, of CO₂ (Mr = 44) in 2.20 g is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: n = mass ÷ Mr = 2.20 ÷ 44 = 0.05 mol. 20 is the upside-down fraction (44 ÷ 2.2) — the error the schemes score 0.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The relative formula mass of Ca(OH)₂ is… [Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1]
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74. The bracket multiplies the whole OH group — forgetting to double the hydrogen gives 73, doubling only the oxygen gives 57.

05-chemical-calculations.q: In an empirical formula calculation you divide each element's % by its…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: By Ar — converting mass to moles of atoms. The 2021 scheme: dividing by atomic numbers scores 0/3.

05-chemical-calculations.q: An element ratio comes out as 1 : 1.33. The empirical formula ratio is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Multiply up, never round: 1.33 = 4/3, so × 3 gives 3 : 4 (this is how 2025's Pb₃O₄ appears). Rounding 1.33 to 1 destroys the question.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The volume of 0.5 mol of any gas at room temperature and pressure is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: One mole of any gas = 24 dm³ at rtp, so 0.5 mol = 12 dm³. (22.4 is the molar volume at STP — a different condition, not used by this spec.)

05-chemical-calculations.q: 6.4 × 10⁶ g of sulfur (Ar = 32) burns to SO₂. The volume of gas at rtp is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Moles = 6.4 × 10⁶ ÷ 32 = 2.0 × 10⁵; × 24 = 4.8 × 10⁶ dm³ — and the paper demanded standard form. Asked identically in 2022 and 2023.

05-chemical-calculations.q: 0.081 g of H₂ (Mr = 2) contains how many molecules? [1 mol = 6.0 × 10²³]
05-chemical-calculations.explain: n = 0.081 ÷ 2 = 0.0405 mol; × 6.0 × 10²³ = 2.43 × 10²² → 2.4 × 10²² to 2 sf. 0.0405 is the moles, not the molecules — read what the question asks for.

05-chemical-calculations.q: Na₂CO₃·xH₂O gives 3.18 g of Na₂CO₃ (Mr 106) and 3.78 g of water on heating. x = ?
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 0.03 mol salt and 0.21 mol water → 1 : 7. This was 2022's crucible practical; 2025's version gave x = 10 with different numbers — the method is identical.

05-chemical-calculations.q: In the water-of-crystallisation practical, x comes out too LOW because…
options: not all the water was driven off
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Left-over water inflates the "anhydrous" mass and shrinks the water figure, so the ratio drops. Fix: reheat to constant mass.

05-chemical-calculations.q: Percentage yield is calculated as…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Both quantities are masses — convert expected moles to grams first. 2025's scheme explicitly rejected dividing the actual mass by the moles figure.

05-chemical-calculations.q: 0.150 mol of PbBr₂ (Mr = 367) is expected; 49.6 g is obtained. The percentage yield is about…
1.5 g of Mg (Ar = 24) needs how many moles of HCl to react completely? (Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂)
05-chemical-calculations.explain: n(Mg) = 0.0625; the 1 : 2 ratio doubles it → 0.125 mol of acid. Comparing this with what's available is how every "show it is in excess" question works.

05-chemical-calculations.q: A compound is 37.8% C, 6.3% H, 55.9% Cl. Its empirical formula is… [C 12, H 1, Cl 35.5]
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 3.15 : 6.3 : 1.57 → ÷ smallest → 2 : 4 : 1 = C₂H₄Cl. C₄H₈Cl₂ is the MOLECULAR formula (when Mr = 127 is given) — know which one is being asked for.

05-chemical-calculations.q: XCO₃ has Mr = 148. The Ar of X is… [C = 12, O = 16]
05-chemical-calculations.explain: CO₃ contributes 12 + 48 = 60, so X = 148 − 60 = 88 → strontium, the Group 2 metal from 2023's question.

05-chemical-calculations.q: Why does a correct final answer with no working still risk zero on these papers?
options: It never does — the answer always scores full marks
Because a wrong answer with no working scores nothing, and error-carried-forward cannot rescue it
Because working is worth more than the answer
05-chemical-calculations.explain: A CORRECT answer without working scores full marks — but one slip with nothing on paper scores zero, because the method marks and ECF have nothing to attach to. Show the moles step.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The Mr of CO₂ is… [C = 12, O = 16]
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 — memorise-level familiar from every gas calculation.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The Mr of (NH₄)₂SO₄ is… [N 14, H 1, S 32, O 16]
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 2 × (14 + 4) = 36, plus 32 + 64 = 96 → 132. The bracket doubles both N and H.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The number of moles in 88 g of CO₂ (Mr = 44) is…
The mass of 0.25 mol of NaOH (Mr = 40) is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: mass = n × Mr = 0.25 × 40 = 10 g. 160 is the upside-down division.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The volume of 2 mol of any gas at rtp is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 2 × 24 = 48 dm³ — molar volume scales with moles, whatever the gas.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The number of moles of gas in 6 dm³ at rtp is…
In 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, 1.5 mol of hydrogen peroxide gives how many moles of oxygen?
05-chemical-calculations.explain: The 2:1 ratio halves it: 0.75 mol — 2024's actual numbers (→ 18 dm³ at rtp).

05-chemical-calculations.q: The % by mass of nitrogen in NH₄NO₃ (Mr = 80) is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: TWO nitrogens: 28 ÷ 80 × 100 = 35%. Counting one N gives the 17.5% trap.

05-chemical-calculations.q: A hydrated salt loses 1.80 g of water (Mr 18) on heating. The moles of water lost are…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 1.80 ÷ 18 = 0.10 mol — the water half of every ·xH₂O calculation.

05-chemical-calculations.q: An oxide of copper contains 3.81 g Cu (Ar 63.5) and 0.96 g O (Ar 16). Its empirical formula is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 0.06 mol of each → 1:1 → CuO. 2024's reduction-practical numbers exactly.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The empirical formula of C₄H₁₀ is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Divide by the highest common factor (2): C₂H₅. Empirical formulae keep whole numbers only.

05-chemical-calculations.q: A compound's empirical formula is CH₂ and its Mr is 56. Its molecular formula is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Empirical mass 14; 56 ÷ 14 = 4 → C₄H₈.

05-chemical-calculations.q: Which sample contains the most molecules?
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Convert to moles: 2, 1, 0.5, 0.5 — the lightest sample wins because moles, not grams, count particles.

05-chemical-calculations.q: 0.02 mol of a salt has a mass of 2.84 g. Its Mr is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Mr = mass ÷ n = 2.84 ÷ 0.02 = 142 (sodium sulfate — 2025's hydrate question used exactly this).

05-chemical-calculations.q: The theoretical yield of a reaction is…
options: the maximum mass the equation predicts
05-chemical-calculations.explain: What the moles route predicts if nothing is lost; % yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.

05-chemical-calculations.q: A reaction's percentage yield is 80% and the theoretical yield is 5.0 g. The actual mass collected is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: actual = 80% of 5.0 = 4.0 g. Rearrange the yield formula confidently in both directions.

05-chemical-calculations.q: Why might a percentage yield be less than 100%? Choose the best reason.
options: Product is lost in filtering, transferring and crystallising
Atoms were destroyed in the reaction
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Physical losses at each step (and side reactions). Atoms are never destroyed — conservation of mass.

05-chemical-calculations.q: 0.5 mol of CaCO₃ decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The volume of CO₂ at rtp is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 1:1 ratio → 0.5 mol of gas → 0.5 × 24 = 12 dm³.

05-chemical-calculations.q: Which conversion is correct?
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ — hence 24 dm³ = 24,000 cm³ for the molar volume.

05-chemical-calculations.q: 4.8 g of magnesium (Ar 24) reacts: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. The moles of O₂ needed are…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: n(Mg) = 0.2; ratio 2:1 → 0.1 mol O₂. Always moles first, then ratio.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The mass of MgO made from 0.2 mol Mg (Mr of MgO = 40) is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 1:1 ratio keeps 0.2 mol; mass = 0.2 × 40 = 8 g.

05-chemical-calculations.q: In a 'show that magnesium is in excess' question, the comparison must be between…
options: the masses of the two reactants
moles needed (via the ratio) and moles available
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Grams of different substances aren't comparable; the equation trades in moles. 2025's show-that was exactly this.

05-chemical-calculations.q: An answer of 2.43 × 10²² asked for to 2 significant figures is written…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Two sig figs: 2.4; keep standard form. The 2024 scheme docked marks for ignoring the printed '2 sf'.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The number of moles of XCO₃ that decompose to give 0.05 mol of CO₂ (XCO₃ → XO + CO₂) is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 1:1 ratio — the moles carry straight across. That step was its own mark in 2023.

05-chemical-calculations.q: Error carried forward (ECF) means…
options: later steps can still score if they use your earlier wrong value correctly
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Why showing working protects you: one slip costs one mark, not the whole question — but only if the method is on the page.

05-chemical-calculations.q: 9 g of water (Mr 18) contains how many molecules? [1 mol = 6.0 × 10²³]
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 0.5 mol × 6.0 × 10²³ = 3.0 × 10²³ molecules.

05-chemical-calculations.q: A gas syringe collects 120 cm³ of gas at rtp. The amount in moles is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: n = 120 ÷ 24,000 = 0.005 mol — match cm³ with 24,000, dm³ with 24.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The Ar values needed for a calculation are found…
options: on the periodic table provided in the exam
from the mass number of the commonest isotope
05-chemical-calculations.explain: The periodic table is given — use the LARGER number in each element's box (the Ar, not the atomic number).

05-chemical-calculations.q: 56 g of iron (Ar 56) and 32 g of sulfur (Ar 32) contain…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 56/56 = 1 and 32/32 = 1 — equal MOLES despite unequal masses. Moles, not grams, count atoms.

05-chemical-calculations.q: A student weighs 27.7 g of salt recovered from 50 g of water. The solubility in g per 100 g is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Double it: 55.4 g per 100 g — the 2024 evaporating-basin numbers (also lives in the Solubility module).

05-chemical-calculations.q: The Mr of MgCl₂ is… [Mg = 24, Cl = 35.5]
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 24 + (2 × 35.5) = 95. Forgetting to double the chlorine gives 59.5 — the commonest slip.

05-chemical-calculations.q: How many moles are in 5.6 g of iron? [Ar Fe = 56]
What mass is 0.2 mol of CaCO₃? [Mr = 100]
In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, how many moles of hydrogen react with 2 mol of nitrogen?
05-chemical-calculations.explain: The ratio is 1 : 3, so 2 mol of N₂ needs 6 mol of H₂ (making 4 mol of NH₃).

05-chemical-calculations.q: The volume of 0.05 mol of gas at rtp, in cm³, is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 0.05 × 24 000 = 1200 cm³ (= 1.2 dm³). Match the molar volume to the unit demanded: 24 dm³ or 24 000 cm³.

05-chemical-calculations.q: A compound contains 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen. Its empirical formula is… [C 12, H 1, O 16]
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 3.33 : 6.7 : 3.33 → divide by the smallest → 1 : 2 : 1 = CH₂O (the glucose empirical formula).

05-chemical-calculations.q: A reaction should yield 8.0 g but produces 6.0 g. The percentage yield is…
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 6.0 ÷ 8.0 × 100 = 75%. Yield can never exceed 100% — an answer above it means the fraction is upside down.

05-chemical-calculations.q: The percentage by mass of oxygen in water is… [H 1, O 16]
05-chemical-calculations.explain: 16 ÷ 18 × 100 = 88.9%. Water is mostly oxygen by MASS even though two-thirds of its atoms are hydrogen.

05-chemical-calculations.q: Which quantity is conserved in every chemical reaction?
05-chemical-calculations.explain: Mass (and atoms) are conserved — the basis of balancing. Molecule counts and volumes change freely.

05-chemical-calculations.q: In a 'show that' calculation, marks are earned by…
options: showing the working that leads to the stated answer
05-chemical-calculations.explain: The answer is already printed — the marks are entirely for the route. This is the one question type where working is literally all there is.

06-solubility.q: A saturated solution is one in which…
options: no more solute can dissolve at that temperature
the solute and solvent have equal masses
no more solute can dissolve at any temperature
06-solubility.explain: The phrase "at that temperature" carries the mark — a solution saturated at 20 °C can dissolve more when warmed.

06-solubility.q: Solubility is measured in…
06-solubility.explain: Grams of solute per 100 g of SOLVENT (water) at a stated temperature — not per 100 g of the finished solution.

06-solubility.q: In salt water, the salt is the…
06-solubility.explain: The solid that dissolves is the solute; the liquid doing the dissolving is the solvent; together they are the solution.

06-solubility.q: The factor that changes how much solid can dissolve in water is…
06-solubility.explain: Temperature changes solubility. Stirring and crushing only change how FAST dissolving happens — the schemes explicitly ignore them.

06-solubility.q: Solubility is 124 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C. The mass dissolving in 250 g of water is…
06-solubility.explain: Scale linearly: 124 × 2.5 = 310 g. (49.6 is the upside-down scaling trap.)

06-solubility.q: A table gives masses dissolving in 25 cm³ of water. To convert to g per 100 g of water…
06-solubility.explain: Four lots of 25 make 100 — and 1 cm³ of water has a mass of 1 g, so cm³ of water and g of water are interchangeable. 2025's conversion step.

06-solubility.q: Solubility is 45 g/100 g at 60 °C and 13 g/100 g at 10 °C. Cooling a saturated solution in 100 g of water from 60 to 10 °C crystallises…
06-solubility.explain: The water keeps 13 g dissolved; the surplus 45 − 13 = 32 g comes out as crystals. Two curve reads and a subtraction — 2023 Q12.

06-solubility.q: When reading a value from a solubility curve in the exam you must…
options: use the nearest curve to your ruler
show the construction lines on the graph
06-solubility.explain: The working lines carry their own mark — 2023, 2024 and 2025 all penalised silent readings. And read the curve the question names.

06-solubility.q: Solubility values measured at 95 °C are less accurate because…
options: some water evaporates during the experiment
saturated solutions cannot exist when hot
06-solubility.explain: Water evaporating means less solvent than recorded, so the calculated solubility drifts high. 2022's one-marker.

06-solubility.q: In the evaporating-basin method, the mixture is filtered before evaporating to…
options: remove the undissolved solid so only saturated solution is measured
06-solubility.explain: Undissolved solid in the basin would be weighed as if it had been dissolved, inflating the answer. Filter first, then evaporate the clear saturated solution to dryness.

06-solubility.q: Why is heating to complete dryness CORRECT in the solubility practical but wrong in salt preparation?
options: Here the goal is a mass measurement, not intact hydrated crystals
Solubility salts contain no water of crystallisation
06-solubility.explain: Purpose decides technique: measuring the total dissolved mass needs everything out of solution; preparing crystals needs the water of crystallisation kept — so there you stop at the crystallisation point.

06-solubility.q: Two solubility curves cross at 68 °C. This means that at 68 °C…
options: the two salts have the same solubility
06-solubility.explain: The crossing point is where the curves share a y-value — equal solubility. Drop a construction line and state the temperature.

06-solubility.q: In sugar dissolved in tea, the solvent is…
06-solubility.explain: The liquid doing the dissolving is the solvent; the sugar is the solute.

06-solubility.q: As temperature rises, the solubility of most solids in water…
06-solubility.explain: Most solubility curves climb with temperature — which is why cooling a saturated solution grows crystals.

06-solubility.q: The mass of water in 40 cm³ of water is…
06-solubility.explain: 1.00 cm³ of water has a mass of 1.00 g — the silent conversion every solubility question uses.

06-solubility.q: A solution holds 30 g of salt per 100 g of water at 40 °C, and the curve reads 48 g at 60 °C. Warming the saturated 40 °C solution to 60 °C means…
06-solubility.explain: Warming raises the ceiling: the solution becomes unsaturated with 18 g of headroom. Crystals only appear on COOLING.

06-solubility.q: Undissolved solid sits at the bottom of a solution. The solution above it is…
06-solubility.explain: Solid remaining at that temperature is the visible proof the solution can hold no more — the practical's test for saturation.

06-solubility.q: The solubility of a gas in water as temperature rises…
06-solubility.explain: Gases behave opposite to solids — warm fizzy drinks go flat. (Background knowledge the school papers have hinted at with dissolved O₂/Cl₂.)

06-solubility.q: 125 g of salt dissolves in 250 g of water at some temperature. The solubility in g per 100 g is…
06-solubility.explain: 125 ÷ 2.5 = 50 g per 100 g — scale DOWN to the standard 100 g.

06-solubility.q: On a solubility curve, a point BELOW the curve represents…
06-solubility.explain: Below the line = less dissolved than the maximum = unsaturated. On the line = saturated; above it, the excess crystallises.

06-solubility.q: Cooling a saturated solution from 70 °C to 10 °C, the mass crystallising equals…
options: the difference between the two solubilities
06-solubility.explain: Hot reading minus cold reading, scaled to the water used — the subtraction that appears every single year.

06-solubility.q: In the solubility practical, the saturated solution is measured by volume then poured into…
06-solubility.explain: Weigh the basin empty FIRST — the whole calculation is differences of basin weighings.

06-solubility.q: Which changes how FAST a solid dissolves but not HOW MUCH dissolves?
06-solubility.explain: Stirring (and crushing) speed things up; only temperature (for a given solute/solvent pair) changes the solubility itself.

06-solubility.q: Two salts have solubilities of 96 g and 55 g per 100 g at 30 °C. In 25 g of water at 30 °C, the first salt can hold…
06-solubility.explain: Scale by the water: 96 ÷ 4 = 24 g. (The second would hold 13.75 g — read which salt is asked!)

06-solubility.q: The best evidence a solution was saturated when filtered is…
options: excess solid was present and removed by the filter
it was stirred for five minutes
06-solubility.explain: Solid left undissolved (then filtered off) proves the solution took all it could.

06-solubility.q: A student's solubility result is higher than the true value. A likely cause is…
options: some water evaporated during the experiment
06-solubility.explain: Lost water → salt credited to less solvent than recorded → inflated g-per-100g. The 95 °C accuracy question in reverse.

06-solubility.q: "Solubility = 36 g per 100 g of water at 25 °C" means…
options: 36 g of water dissolves 100 g of salt
100 g of water is saturated by 36 g of salt at 25 °C
06-solubility.explain: Read the units in order: grams of SOLUTE per 100 g of SOLVENT, at the stated temperature.

06-solubility.q: Why must the temperature be stated with any solubility value?
06-solubility.explain: The number is meaningless without it — the same salt might hold 13 g at 10 °C and 45 g at 60 °C.

06-solubility.q: The five steps F(water) G(add salt) B(filter) H(pour) A(evaporate) are in the practical's order. Which step guarantees saturation?
options: G — adding salt until no more dissolves
06-solubility.explain: Adding with stirring UNTIL NO MORE DISSOLVES is the saturation step; everything after just measures what dissolved.

06-solubility.q: Cooling crystallisation is used in salt preparation because…
options: solubility falls on cooling, forcing pure crystals out of solution
06-solubility.explain: The falling curve pushes salt out as well-formed crystals while impurities stay behind in the liquor — chemistry's cleanest purification.

06-solubility.q: 20 g of salt is dissolved in 50 g of water and 4 g remains undissolved after stirring at 20 °C. The solubility at 20 °C is…
06-solubility.explain: Dissolved = 16 g in 50 g of water → × 2 = 32 g per 100 g.

06-solubility.q: Which line on a graph of solubility vs temperature is typical for a solid salt?
06-solubility.explain: Solids nearly always dissolve better hot — the standard rising curve of KNO₃ and friends.

06-solubility.q: What happens to the solubility of most solids as the water is heated?
06-solubility.explain: Most solids dissolve better hot — the rising solubility curve. Gases do the opposite.

06-solubility.q: A solution that can still dissolve more solute is described as…
06-solubility.explain: Unsaturated = below the curve. Saturated = on the curve, holding the maximum for that temperature.

06-solubility.q: 60 g of salt dissolves in 200 g of water. The solubility in g per 100 g is…
06-solubility.explain: Halve it to standardise to 100 g of water: 30 g per 100 g.

06-solubility.q: Crystals form when a saturated solution cools because…
options: the solubility falls, so the excess solute comes out of solution
06-solubility.explain: The ceiling drops as it cools; whatever no longer fits crystallises out. That is both the exam calculation and the purification method.

06-solubility.q: In the solubility practical, filtering the mixture before evaporating removes…
06-solubility.explain: Only the saturated solution should be weighed; undissolved solid would be counted as if it had dissolved and inflate the result.

06-solubility.q: Which is the correct unit for solubility?
06-solubility.explain: The spec's unit: grams of solute per 100 g of solvent, at a stated temperature.

06-solubility.q: Two curves cross at 40 °C. Below 40 °C, the salt with the higher curve is…
06-solubility.explain: Higher on the graph = more grams dissolve per 100 g. The crossing point is the single temperature where they match.

06-solubility.q: Why must a solubility figure always state a temperature?
06-solubility.explain: The same salt might hold 13 g at 10 °C and 45 g at 60 °C — the number is meaningless without its temperature.

06-solubility.q: A saturated solution at 80 °C is cooled to 20 °C. Solubility falls from 90 to 30 g/100 g. Using 100 g of water, the mass crystallising is…
06-solubility.explain: 90 − 30 = 60 g. Hot reading minus cold reading — then scale if the water is not 100 g.

06-solubility.q: Stirring a mixture makes the solid dissolve faster. This means stirring changes the…
06-solubility.explain: Speed, not amount. Only temperature (for a given pair) changes how much can dissolve — the schemes ignore stirring in solubility answers.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: A catalyst increases the rate of reaction by…
options: providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Both halves needed: alternative pathway AND lower activation energy. "Lowers the activation energy" alone lost a mark in 2025.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Increasing the concentration of a solution increases the rate because…
options: there are more particles per unit volume so collisions are more frequent
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Concentration is about crowding, not energy — the 2024 scheme capped any kinetic-energy answer at 1 of 3. Frequency of collisions is the required phrase.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Increasing temperature increases the rate mainly because…
options: more collisions have energy above the activation energy
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: A greater proportion of collisions are successful — that is the dominant effect, with more frequent collisions as the minor one. The activation energy itself never changes with temperature.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: In a rate experiment measured on a balance, the cotton wool plug is there to…
options: stop acid spray escaping so the mass loss is only the gas
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The gas MUST escape or the mass would never change — the plug only holds back the spray. "Prevents gas escaping" was explicitly rejected in 2022.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The reaction stops while marble chips remain in the flask because…
options: the cotton wool blocked the reaction
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Visible solid left over means the OTHER reactant ran out — the acid is limiting. The balance shows it: the mass stops changing.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The rate of reaction AT 60 seconds is found from…
options: the total mass change divided by 60
the gradient of a tangent drawn at 60 s
the average of the first and last readings
the y-value of the curve at 60 s
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Rate at an instant = tangent gradient. Total-change ÷ time is the AVERAGE rate — it scored 1 of 3 in 2022.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: A correct unit for a rate of reaction is…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Volume per time or mass per time: cm³/min, cm³/s, g/s. 2025's commentary: "m is meters!" — write min for minutes, and cm³ not cm.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Powdered marble reacts faster than the same mass of chips because the powder has…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: More particles exposed at the surface → more frequent collisions. Solids never have a "concentration" — that word cost a mark in 2023.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Compared with the original curve, the volume–time curve at a higher temperature is…
options: steeper and levels off at the same volume
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Faster journey, same destination — the amounts of reactant are unchanged, so the plateau height is unchanged. A raised plateau means you changed the AMOUNT, not the rate.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The activation energy is…
options: the energy released by a reaction
the minimum energy colliding particles need to react
the average energy of the particles
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The minimum collision energy for reaction. Successful collision = one at or above it.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: A catalyst is chemically unchanged at the end of a reaction. The evidence is…
options: its mass is the same before and after
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Filter, dry, reweigh: same mass — and it will catalyse a fresh run just as well. That is the definition's second half: increases the rate, chemically unchanged at the end.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: In the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, manganese(IV) oxide acts as…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ happens slowly on its own; MnO₂ speeds it up and is recovered unchanged. The school's set catalyst practical (spec 3.16).

07-rates-of-reaction.q: "More successful collisions" alone was not enough for the temperature mark in 2023. The full answer also needs…
options: a greater PROPORTION of collisions successful, separate from frequency
